# Attribution Report: Guccifer 2.0, DCLeaks, and GRU-Controlled Election-Interference Operations

## Executive Summary

The available evidence supports a strong attribution chain connecting the Guccifer 2.0 and DCLeaks personas to a broader Russian military-intelligence operation targeting the 2016 U.S. presidential election. The strongest source is the July 2018 federal indictment, which alleges that officers of Russia’s Main Intelligence Directorate (GRU), particularly personnel assigned to Units 26165 and 74455, hacked campaign and Democratic Party systems, stole documents, created the DCLeaks and Guccifer 2.0 personas, and used those personas to release or transfer stolen material. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2018](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election))

CrowdStrike’s incident-response account provides independent technical and forensic context. It reports that two Russian intelligence-affiliated adversaries—COZY BEAR and FANCY BEAR—were present in the Democratic National Committee (DNC) network, with FANCY BEAR associated with X-Agent and X-Tunnel malware. CrowdStrike also describes the use of credential phishing, malware, persistence mechanisms, command-and-control infrastructure, log clearing, and data exfiltration indicators. ([CrowdStrike, 2016/2020](https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/bears-midst-intrusion-democratic-national-committee/))

The evidence is not identical in form or scope. The indictment is a prosecutorial allegation rather than a judicial finding, while CrowdStrike’s account is an incident-response and threat-intelligence assessment rather than a complete public evidentiary record. CrowdStrike also states that it did not observe exfiltration in real time and lacked “concrete evidence” in the narrow sensor-based sense, although it concluded from indicators and circumstantial evidence that data left the network. These limitations do not materially undermine the attribution chain; instead, they clarify the different evidentiary bases used by the two sources.

**Overall assessment:** The most reasonable conclusion from the supplied evidence is that Guccifer 2.0 and DCLeaks were operational personas used within, or in direct support of, a GRU-linked election-interference campaign. The attribution is strongest when assessed cumulatively through identity linkage, infrastructure overlap, financing overlap, operational timing, malware relationships, and the transfer of stolen material to Organization 1.

## Sources and Evidentiary Status

| Source ID | Source | Evidentiary character |
|---|---|---|
| S1 | U.S. Department of Justice indictment, July 13, 2018 | Grand-jury indictment and prosecutorial allegations |
| S2 | CrowdStrike, “Bears in the Midst: Intrusion Into the Democratic National Committee,” with later updates | Incident-response account, technical assessment, and clarification of evidentiary limitations |

The distinction between allegation and established fact is important. S1 states that the named defendants “were GRU officers” and describes their alleged conduct, but the document is an indictment. It should therefore be reported as an allegation or government assertion, not as a conviction or adjudicated finding. S2 is a company-authored technical account by the organization that investigated the DNC intrusion. It contains direct statements about what CrowdStrike observed, together with analytical judgments about actor identity and Russian government affiliation.

## The Attribution Chain

### 1. The underlying operation was attributed to GRU units

S1 identifies GRU Units 26165 and 74455 as Russian military-intelligence units involved in cyber operations and staged releases of stolen documents. The indictment alleges that Unit 26165 had primary responsibility for hacking the DCCC, DNC, and email accounts associated with the Clinton campaign, while Unit 74455 assisted with document releases, promotion, social-media activity, and related infrastructure. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2018](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election))

This division is analytically significant. It separates the intrusion and collection function from the public-disclosure and influence function. The indictment does not describe Guccifer 2.0 or DCLeaks as independent actors merely exploiting material obtained elsewhere. Instead, it alleges that the personas were constructed and operated as components of the same broader campaign.

### 2. DCLeaks was allegedly constructed before public document releases

According to S1, the conspirators registered **dcleaks.com** on or about April 19, 2016, more than a month before the site publicly released documents. The domain was allegedly registered through an anonymizing service and funded through cryptocurrency. The indictment further alleges that the email account used to register the domain was also connected to the URL-shortening account used in spearphishing operations against the Clinton campaign chairman and other campaign personnel. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2018](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election))

This creates a direct infrastructure linkage between:

1. credential theft targeting Clinton campaign personnel;
2. the creation of DCLeaks; and
3. the later publication of stolen emails.

S1 alleges that DCLeaks launched publicly on June 8, 2016, and falsely represented itself as the work of American hacktivists. It also alleges that the operators used fictitious U.S. identities—including “Alice Donovan,” “Jason Scott,” and “Richard Gingrey”—to promote the website through social-media accounts. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2018](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election))

The implication is not merely that DCLeaks published politically useful material. The indictment alleges advance planning, false persona construction, infrastructure concealment, social-media promotion, and integration with the hacking operation.

### 3. Guccifer 2.0 emerged immediately after public attribution of the DNC intrusion

S1 alleges that the DNC publicly announced on June 14, 2016 that Russian government actors had hacked its network. The indictment then states that the conspirators created Guccifer 2.0 in response and falsely claimed that the persona was a lone Romanian hacker. The alleged purpose was to undermine claims of Russian government responsibility. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2018](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election))

The timing is a central attribution indicator. On June 15, 2016, S1 alleges that conspirators logged into a Moscow-based server used and managed by Unit 74455 and searched for phrases that subsequently appeared in Guccifer 2.0’s first blog post. The indictment alleges that the post was published later that day and reproduced several of the searched phrases, including language concerning the security company, “some hundred sheets,” and whether the company’s competence should be questioned. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2018](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election))

This sequence provides a distinctive operational link:

- Moscow-based server associated in the indictment with Unit 74455;
- searches for wording relevant to the public narrative;
- publication of the first Guccifer 2.0 message shortly afterward;
- use of language apparently prepared or selected during the preceding server session.

Standing alone, linguistic overlap would not prove authorship. In combination with the alleged server access, timing, infrastructure overlap, and later transfers of stolen data, it substantially strengthens the attribution.

### 4. The personas allegedly used overlapping infrastructure and financing

S1 alleges that Guccifer 2.0 and DCLeaks used overlapping computer infrastructure and financing. Specifically, the indictment states that the same pool of bitcoin funds was used to purchase a virtual private network account and lease a Malaysian server. The Malaysian server allegedly hosted dcleaks.com, while the VPN was later used to access the @Guccifer_2 Twitter account. The same infrastructure was also allegedly used to register malicious domains associated with the hacking of the DCCC and DNC. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2018](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election))

The indictment further alleges that the conspirators used bitcoin mining, peer-to-peer exchanges, prepaid cards, multiple email accounts, fictitious names, and layered transactions to acquire infrastructure while obscuring their identities and Russian government connections. It places the total amount laundered for this infrastructure at more than $95,000. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2018](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election))

This evidence is important because it links the personas at the operational—not merely thematic—level. Common political messaging could be copied by unaffiliated actors. Shared VPN access, servers, domain-registration infrastructure, and funding pools are more difficult to explain as coincidence.

### 5. Guccifer 2.0 allegedly transferred material to Organization 1

S1 alleges that Guccifer 2.0 transferred stolen DNC and Clinton campaign materials to Organization 1, identified in the indictment without naming it. The parties allegedly discussed timing and the political impact of releases. Organization 1 reportedly requested new Hillary Clinton-related material before the Democratic National Convention and stated that such material would have a “much higher impact.” ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2018](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election))

The indictment alleges that an encrypted file containing access instructions was sent on July 14, 2016, that Organization 1 confirmed receipt of approximately one gigabyte of data, and that it released more than 20,000 emails and other documents on July 22, 2016. It further alleges that approximately 33 tranches of Clinton campaign chairman emails were released between October 7 and November 7, 2016, totaling more than 50,000 documents. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2018](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election))

This alleged handoff explains the relationship between the persona-level activity and the larger publication operation: Guccifer 2.0 was not only a public-facing identity but also, according to the indictment, a transfer mechanism for stolen data.

## Incident-Response Corroboration

### CrowdStrike’s technical findings

CrowdStrike states that it was contacted by the DNC on April 30, 2016 and began investigating on May 1. It reports identifying two separate adversaries on the network: COZY BEAR and FANCY BEAR. CrowdStrike associates FANCY BEAR with X-Agent and X-Tunnel, malware families also identified in S1’s description of the GRU intrusion. ([CrowdStrike, 2016/2020](https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/bears-midst-intrusion-democratic-national-committee/))

CrowdStrike describes FANCY BEAR as a Russian-based threat actor associated with targeted intrusions and possibly linked to the GRU. It identifies X-Agent capabilities including remote command execution, file transmission, and keylogging, and describes X-Tunnel as a network-tunneling tool. ([CrowdStrike, 2016/2020](https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/bears-midst-intrusion-democratic-national-committee/))

S1 independently describes X-Agent and X-Tunnel as GRU malware. It alleges that X-Agent was used to monitor DCCC and DNC computers, capture keystrokes and screenshots, steal credentials, and maintain access, while X-Tunnel was used to move stolen documents through encrypted channels. ([U.S. Department of Justice, 2018](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election))

The malware overlap is therefore a significant corroborating feature:

| Technical element | S1 indictment | S2 CrowdStrike account |
|---|---|---|
| X-Agent | Described as GRU malware used for monitoring, keylogging, screenshots, and persistence | Associated with FANCY BEAR and used for command execution, file transmission, and keylogging |
| X-Tunnel | Used to move stolen documents outside DCCC/DNC networks | Described as a network-tunneling tool |
| Credential theft | Spearphishing, stolen passwords, and credential reuse | Spearphishing and credential-acquisition activity |
| Anti-forensics | Log deletion and attempts to remove traces | Event-log clearing and timestamp manipulation |
| Russian attribution | GRU Units 26165 and 74455 | Russian intelligence-affiliated adversaries; FANCY BEAR possibly linked to GRU |

### Limits of the CrowdStrike evidence

CrowdStrike expressly states that it did not see the adversaries exfiltrate data in real time. It says it had indicators and circumstantial evidence, rather than a network sensor directly recording every transfer. ([CrowdStrike, 2016/2020](https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/bears-midst-intrusion-democratic-national-committee/))

This is not a contradiction with S1. The sources address different questions:

- S2 describes what the incident responders directly observed and inferred from forensic artifacts.
- S1 presents the government’s broader investigative allegations, including alleged server activity, cryptocurrency transactions, persona operations, and later document releases.

The difference should be stated precisely: CrowdStrike’s public account does not independently establish every detail alleged in the indictment, particularly the identity of the individuals operating Guccifer 2.0 and DCLeaks. Conversely, the indictment’s persona and infrastructure allegations do not convert CrowdStrike’s limited direct observation into real-time proof. Together, however, they form mutually reinforcing evidence.

## Contradictions and Apparent Tensions

### Different actor labels

CrowdStrike describes COZY BEAR and FANCY BEAR, while S1 identifies GRU Units 26165 and 74455. These are not necessarily contradictory classifications. They are different naming systems: S2 uses threat-intelligence actor labels, while S1 uses military-unit attribution. The supplied evidence supports an association between FANCY BEAR and GRU-linked X-Agent/X-Tunnel activity, but it does not provide a complete formal crosswalk from every CrowdStrike label to every GRU unit.

### “Concrete evidence” versus alleged theft

CrowdStrike says it lacked concrete, direct sensor evidence of exfiltration, while S1 alleges that GRU officers stole thousands of documents. These statements can coexist because they concern different evidentiary records and standards. CrowdStrike’s limitation concerns what its own responders directly observed; S1 reflects the government’s larger investigative record.

### Public persona claims versus attribution

Guccifer 2.0 allegedly claimed to be a lone Romanian hacker, and DCLeaks allegedly claimed to be operated by American hacktivists. S1 characterizes those claims as false. Because the source is an indictment, that characterization should be reported as an allegation. Nevertheless, the alleged Moscow-server activity, shared infrastructure, shared financing, and transfer of stolen documents provide a coherent explanation for why the identities were presented deceptively.

## Conclusion

The evidence supports a concrete attribution judgment: **Guccifer 2.0 and DCLeaks were most likely operational personas associated with a GRU-controlled or GRU-directed election-interference campaign, rather than independent hackers acting without Russian military-intelligence coordination.**

The conclusion rests on several mutually reinforcing elements:

1. S1 attributes the hacking and release operation to GRU Units 26165 and 74455.
2. S1 links DCLeaks infrastructure to credential-theft infrastructure used against Clinton campaign personnel.
3. S1 places Guccifer 2.0’s creation immediately after the public disclosure of Russian involvement.
4. S1 alleges that a Moscow-based server managed by Unit 74455 was used shortly before Guccifer 2.0’s first post.
5. S1 alleges shared VPN, server, domain, and bitcoin-financing infrastructure between Guccifer 2.0 and DCLeaks.
6. S1 alleges that Guccifer 2.0 transferred stolen material to Organization 1 for timed publication.
7. S2 independently identifies Russian intelligence-affiliated activity in the DNC network and associates the relevant malware with FANCY BEAR and GRU-linked tradecraft.

The appropriate qualification is that the indictment contains allegations, not a criminal judgment, and CrowdStrike’s public account has acknowledged limits concerning direct observation of exfiltration. Those qualifications reduce certainty about specific operational details but do not substantially weaken the cumulative attribution assessment.

## References

CrowdStrike. (2016, June 14; updated 2020, June 4). *Bears in the Midst: Intrusion Into the Democratic National Committee; CrowdStrike’s work with the Democratic National Committee: Setting the record straight*. CrowdStrike. [https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/bears-midst-intrusion-democratic-national-committee/](https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/blog/bears-midst-intrusion-democratic-national-committee/)

U.S. Department of Justice. (2018, July 13). *Grand jury indicts 12 Russian intelligence officers for hacking offenses related to the 2016 election: United States v. Viktor Borisovich Netyksho et al., Criminal No. 18-cr-00215-ABJ*. [https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/grand-jury-indicts-12-russian-intelligence-officers-hacking-offenses-related-2016-election)
